newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW-Dutch credit insurer NCM sees '96 profit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Dutch credit insurer NCM sees '96 profit.

text.p: Dutch credit insurer NCM, one of the five biggest credit insurers in Europe, said its full year 1996 result would be much the same as the 13.8 million guilders it earned in the first six months of the year.
"The 1996 result will be comparable to the profit we made in the first half of the year," chairman Maarten Hulshoff said in an interview.
The 1996 result will be published on May 29.
In 1995 NCM announced a loss of 5.9 million guilders.
NCM, established about 70 years ago, is jointly owned by Dutch banks and insurers and some foreign reinsurers.
It normally makes a profit in the first half of the year because of the way it accounts for claims.
Hulshoff, who became chairman about 18 months ago, said NCM was aiming for average turnover growth of at least seven percent per year. "Growth in profits should exceed this," Hulshof said.
NCM's value of business insured amounts to some 200 billion guilders per year.
He said it was trying to expand business by widening its client base.

"Before, we were focusing on companies in the middle segment -- international corporates -- to sell credit insurance policies to," Hulshoff said. He said NCM would focus more on smaller companies and global players in future.
NCM recently divided its firm in three units.
They are the on-line unit, which will focus on small companies, the corporate unit, in which it already has a strong presence, and a global unit for multinationals.
"There is an urgent need for credit insurance for smaller companies as it had not been broadly available for a long time," Hulshoff said.
He said policies for smaller companies were unprofitable previously but should be profitable in the new system.
Hulshoff said NCM was mainly using telephone-sales in the smaller companies segment to lower costs.
It was already insuring some 15 percent of total Dutch exports, around 12 percent of total British exports and more than one quarter of all Danish exports.
Hulshoff said he did not see much growth in the middle-segment (corporates) as its penetration rate was already somewhere between 18 and 21 percent.
"Growth should come from the left (smaller companies) or the right (global players)," he said.
He said NCM was not planning any mergers to boost growth.
"Organic growth is usually the best," he said.
Hulshoff saw extra growth from the launch of the euro and the founding of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The EMU and euro will have a positive impact on trading flows," Hulshoff said, adding that this would also boost the amount of business that needed to be insured.
Hulshoff said NCM's claims were largest in Germany and in the textile industry.
"The damage in Germany (for credit insurances) is among the highest worldwide," he said.
NCM had also received claims from exporters as a result of BSE, or mad cow disease, and the outbreak of swine fever, but he declined to specify the damage for NCM as result of this.
"It is not alarming," he said.
